claim: YouTube disclosed in September 2022 that it had paid creators, artists and media companies over $50 billion over the preceding three years and that the YouTube Partner Program had over 2 million partners.
stance_target: Platform payouts to creators are large in aggregate
scope_conditions: Platform-disclosed, self-reported and unaudited; the $50B figure is footnoted 'As of June 2022' and covers roughly mid-2019 to mid-2022; critically it aggregates independent creators WITH artists and media companies, so it cannot be divided by partner count to infer creator earnings; no distribution, median or country breakdown is disclosed
quoted_support: Over the past three years, we've paid creators, artists and media companies over $50B.

claim: YouTube has never published a distribution of creator earnings alongside its aggregate payout figures, disclosing only totals and partner counts, which makes the median YouTube creator's income unknowable from platform-disclosed data.
stance_target: That platform payout disclosures answer the question of what share of creators earn a living wage
scope_conditions: Audited absence, based on YouTube's flagship monetization announcement of September 2022; a naive $50B / 2M partners / 3 years arithmetic yields roughly $8,300 per partner per year, but that calculation is invalid because the numerator includes record labels and media companies and the denominator is a headcount at a single point in time
quoted_support: This unique business model means we only succeed when our creators do. And creators are succeeding, these creator entrepreneurs are building successful businesses of their own with employees and full-fledged operations.

claim: YouTube's monetization eligibility thresholds as of September 2022 were 1,000 subscribers plus 4,000 watch hours for long-form, with a new Shorts pathway of 1,000 subscribers plus 10 million Shorts views over 90 days opening in early 2023 and a 45% revenue share on Shorts.
stance_target: Where the monetization floor sits and why creator cohorts before and after 2023 are not comparable
scope_conditions: Platform-disclosed policy, September 2022, global; thresholds have changed repeatedly, which is precisely why attrition and income cohorts spanning threshold changes cannot be compared directly
quoted_support: Starting in early 2023, Shorts-focused creators can apply to YPP by meeting a threshold of 1,000 subscribers and 10M Shorts views over 90 days.
